openingMessage: Own your response. Own your equipment. Own your preparation. Own your outcome. Stay disciplined. Stay prepared. Protect each other. Let's go to work.
openingWhy: This week our own trailer checks caught a low SABA, an empty one, and an SCBA out of hydro — before one hand staked his lungs on any of them. Ownership isn't a poster on the wall. It's a bottle that's full because somebody checked it.
leadershipThought: Know your anchor point is rated for your fall distance before you step off the platform. A dropped tool at 20 feet hits hard. Tether it before you climb, not after.

specialFocus.title: Midweek: Monday and Tuesday's Wins and Misses, Then Working at Height on the Rig-Up
specialFocus.why:
Ray, midweek check. Here's what Matt Croom's reviews of Sunday's, Monday's and Tuesday's forms showed. Say the names, fix the misses, then take Working at Height to the place we're most often off the ground: rig-ups and rig-downs.

✓ THE GOOD: say these names
  • Jordan Lemmons, trailer 152 (Mon): heard a wheel bearing making noise, brought the trailer back, and wrote down who was told. The problem, the action and the name: that's the whole habit.
  • Michael Jobe, Calverley-McDaniels (Mon): the crew had no tag line, so Jobe had them get one before the work. Second week running he's fixed the setup first (cones on Saturday).
  • Nathan Contreras (Tue): the only tech with nothing to fix. Two inspections on trailer 604, two air jobs, full close-outs, every photo from that day. He was on Matt's clean list four days last week too. Jerry Gonzales was close behind on trailer 602 and Kewanee C #1.
  • Humberto Marquez-Salazar, trailer 606 (Tue): three inspections plus the readiness form, FR on every one, every photo from that day. The heaviest clean trailer record of the day.
  • Brianda Sandoval, trailer 603 (Sun): the only complete trailer set of the day. Two inspections and the readiness form, pressure and hydro date on every bottle, every photo from that day.
  • Tyrell Sanders, Fred B Houston #4, and Kedrick McCarter, Allar Callaway (Mon): full OWL close-outs with real narratives and same-day photos.
  • Read the Bottle is sticking: every charged bottle had both pressure and hydro date on 602, 605 and 507 Monday, and on 601, 603, 605, 606 and 607 Tuesday.
✗ THE MISSES: fix these today
  • Still zero "utilized" ticks Sunday through Tuesday. Getting a crew to fetch a tag line before the work is a stop. Tick utilized and write two lines.
  • Tick what happened, then write it. Tuesday, three forms ticked "unsafe conditions" with nothing unsafe in the write-up, and the one form that described a real hazard (a flooded, muddy location, handled before work) didn't tick it.
  • Copied selections. Monday, the same long "what did we observe" list was identical on five forms and the same "what went well" list on eight. Tuesday, five forms had those lists empty. Pick fresh for each job. That's how the office knows what actually happened.
  • Trailer forms. By 11 PM Monday, only 3 of 12 air trailers had the full set: two inspections plus the readiness form. Tuesday, six assigned trailers were still short an inspection or the readiness form.
  • Old photos. Stale ELSA and alarm photos on the H2S daily every day, a rig-down and a rig-up with photos from 2021, and Tuesday a job whose JSA and gas log photos were from 2020.
  • Problem written, nobody named. Tuesday, a broken cascade rack weld and missing caution tape were written up with no one named. Write what's wrong and who you told.
  • Rig gear and counts. One rig-up went out without its repeater, three rig forms had equipment counts that disagree between the top of the form and the checklist, and Tuesday a rig check was filed twice with opposite answers on the alarm test. Count it once, count it right, before you leave the yard.
On the office, not the crew: crews were still asking for mask bags, stickers and caution tape this week, and one contractor still reports no FR coveralls issued. We owe you both.
specialFocus.standardLabel: Working at Height on Rig-Ups and Rig-Downs
standard: Plan the climb before you load the truck. Sensor heads, windsocks, repeaters and alarms often go up high. Know where each one goes and how you'll reach it.
Six feet or more, measured from where you'd land: 100% tied off to an approved anchor. If you can't name the anchor, you don't have one.
Inspect your harness and lanyard before you put them on. Damaged gear comes out of service.
Hands free on the stairs and ladders, three points of contact. Tools and equipment go up in a bag or on a line, and they're tethered while you work.
Nobody under you. Tell the rig crew you're working overhead and keep the area below clear.
Name your rescue before you go up. Who gets you down, and how?

scenarios.title: Hanging the Windsock
scenarios.body: Rig-up day, and the windsock goes on a bracket up the stairs. You're at the top, and the bracket is just out of reach past the handrail. One foot on the bottom rail and you'd have it. Stop there. Standing on the rail puts you above the guardrail, and you're working at height with nothing to catch you. Come down, get your harness, find a rated anchor or a better way to reach it, and send the sock up on a line. Ray, ask the circle: what's the reach on your last rig-up that you almost made without tying off?

questions: On your last rig-up, what did you install above six feet, and what did you tie off to?
If a tool slipped from where you were working overhead, who was standing below?
Jordan heard a bearing and brought the trailer back. What have you heard or felt at a hookup that you drove on anyway?
Who gets you down if you go over today? Name them.
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Above six feet you're tied off, your tools are tethered and the people below know you're up there. On every form, write what's wrong and who you told, and tick the stop when you use it.
